newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Zapata steps down as Guatemala central bank chief.
newsitem.headline: Zapata steps down as Guatemala central bank chief.

text.p: Willy W. Zapata on Thursday said he was stepping down as head of Guatemala's central bank after his current term expires June 30.
He was being replaced by economist Edin Velasquez.
Zapata, 40, told Reuters he had decided against seeking an extension to his four-year term as architect of national fiscal policy because of personal reasons.
"For personal reasons and a change of activity, I made the decision to leave. I talked to the president of the republic and we agreed," he said in an interview.
A Bank of Guatemala spokesman said Velasquez, 49, director of Construcredit Group, will succeed Zapata on July 2. Guatemala's Military Day public holiday is on July 1.

Velasquez will take over as president of the central bank and the monetary board, whose private and public sector members advise the Guatemalan president and set monetary policy. The Bank of Guatemala controls reserves and influences interest rates.

Zapata, who began his two-decade career with the bank as a teller, cited a constitutional amendment forbidding the bank from giving credit to the government as the greatest accomplishment of his tenure.
"That has been very important in giving a sign to the market about the orientation of central bank policy," he said.
Further legislative and constitutional changes are needed to ensure the bank's autonomy and bring it into compliance with the Basle accord regulating international banking.
Jorge Jacobs, executive director of Guatemala's Center for Economic-Social Studies, a think tank, said Zapata had been extremely effective in implementing Monetary Board policy.
But he said inflation during Zapata's tenure remained high, averaging between 10 and 12 percent.
Zapata countered that inflation has dropped to about nine percent from 14 percent when he took office, though he agreed on the need to reduce it further.
Velasquez, named by Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu, worked for 21 years at the Bank of Guatemala, serving as vice president from 1991 to 1993.
"His formation is in the central bank; he is not a politician," Bank of Guatemala spokesman Enrique Amurrio said.
After leaving the Bank of Guatemala in 1993, he was hired as vice president of Construcredit Group's Construction Bank, rising to executive director of the corporation.
Jacobs said monetary policy probably would change little under Velasquez, given that the Monetary Board's decisions were based on a consensus of members and not set by its president.
Later this year Zapata will take up a position as chief executive of a private finance group, which he declined to name.
He is the first Bank of Guatemala president in more than two decades to complete the four-year term, Amurrio said.
"He broke a contemporary record," he said.
